messages.subject: Variable WAIC values
parts:
Hello everyone

 

I am running into the problem of variable WAIC values and infinite DIC values while running a logistic regression with spatial correlation. I am using the package geostatsp (which is based on INLA) to make it easier to include spatial correlation in a logistic regression. I have few observations (n = 101 with 0 or 1 responses) and several variables that don't seem to explain much. I use the function glgm from the geostatsp package which implements a Matern2D model.

 

Using the inla.rerun function, I run the same model several times and obtain very different results for WAIC. From what I read, tiny variations are expected in the values because of parallelization, but I expect that it should lead to much smaller variations. In a similar question, the suggestion was to reduce model complexity or use tighter priors. Reducing model complexity is not much of an option and my current priors are what was felt to be appropriate. Tightening priors does indeed lead to much less variable WAIC values and I understand that my priors might be a bit wide considering the small amount of data.

 

Then, my questions are, am I asking too much from INLA considering the small data? Is my only option tightening priors? Could it be a bug in INLA? Below is the code and the different values obtained.

 

Thanks for your time,

François

 


library(geostatsp)

library(INLA)

library(sp)

library(rgdal)

 

fit<-glgm(y ~ f + x1 + x2,

          data = ds,

          grid = 20,

          covariates = NULL,

          family = "binomial",

          buffer = 10000,

          shape = 1,

          priorCI = list(sd = c(0.4,4), range = c(2000, 50000)),

          control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, dic = TRUE)

)

 

for(i in 1:10){

  m <- inla.rerun(fit$inla)

  print(c(m$waic$waic, m$dic$dic))

}

Hi,

unstable WAIC and DIC is a symptom of something else, and as you
implicitely suggest, weak data is the source. and the results are
supersensitive for minor changes, and the posterior is likely flat over
a large area as well, and you see how this goes.
you can compensate for this using stronger priors, which might be a
good thing to do in these case, maybe with a contraction to a simpler
model (PC-priors: statistical science 2017)

Just adding a bit of information that may shed some more light on this problem.
When setting the number of threads used to 1, the WAIC values stabilize
(but the DICs are still infinite). From the INLA log file, the default value for num.threads
in geostatsp seems to be to use all cores contrary to the default value of 1 for INLA
on Windows. I haven't decided on stronger priors or played with pc priors yet...

François

fit <- glgm(y ~ f + x1 + x2,

data = ds,
               grid = 20,
               covariates = NULL,
               family = "binomial",
               buffer = 10000,
               shape = 1,

priorCI = list(sd = c(0.4, 4), range = c(2000, 50000)),
               control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, dic = TRUE),
               num.threads = 1

)

for(i in 1:10){
   m <- inla.rerun(fit$inla)
   print(c(m$waic$waic, m$dic$dic))
 }
